canonical_statement: The report assessed morbidity and mortality from thromboembolic complications occurring during and after anticoagulant treatment of patients with deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism from 1945 through 1964.
The analysis included 2,027 episodes of lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in 1,744 patients.

population.label: Patients with episodes of lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism

canonical_statement: The study excluded superficial venous thrombosis of the arms or legs, venous obstruction by neoplasm, and deep venous thrombosis of the upper extremity.

inclusion_criteria: Lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
exclusion_criteria: Superficial venous thrombosis of arms or legs

canonical_statement: Recommended treatment during the study period consisted of initial heparinization until Quick prothrombin activity reached therapeutic levels, followed by oral anticoagulants for at least 7 days.

exposures.details: Initial heparinization until Quick prothrombin activity reached therapeutic levels

canonical_statement: The mean duration of anticoagulant therapy in the hospital was 16 days with a standard deviation of 11 days.

Any new sign or symptom compatible with deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or pulmonary infarction that appeared after the first dose of heparin or oral anticoagulant was classified as a thromboembolic complication.
Five patients who were terminally ill from lethal pulmonary embolism when first seen and died within 24 hours after only one or two heparin doses were excluded from the mortality analysis.
Of the 2,027 treatment episodes, 1,735 had some follow-up and 1,371 had follow-up for at least 12 weeks.

Follow-up for at least 12 weeks was available for 88% of courses with post-treatment complications but only 63% of courses without subsequent complications, creating potential bias in estimated post-treatment complication incidence.

Post-treatment complication frequency was estimated using the 1,735 episodes with some follow-up, assuming that patients lost before 12 weeks had complication rates similar to those observed and that patients totally lost to follow-up had as many complications as those under observation.
Among 639 treatment courses with pulmonary embolism as the initial diagnosis, 31 pulmonary embolic complications occurred during hospital treatment (4.9%).

canonical_statement: No detectable influence of initial heparin treatment on complication frequency was observed; interpretation was limited because 906 of 1,289 heparin-treated episodes received heparin for 48 hours or less.

Beginning in July 1956, a prospective randomized study assigned patients according to whether the last digit of the hospital registration number was odd or even to a Quick prothrombin activity target of 10-29% or 30-49%.

In the randomized intensity comparison among courses with pulmonary embolism as the initial diagnosis, thromboembolic complications occurred in 6 of 196 courses (3.0%) with a Quick prothrombin activity target of 10-29% versus 13 of 174 courses (7.4%) with a target of 30-49%; chi-square was 3.55 with 0.05 < p < 0.10.

canonical_statement: Clinical and routine-autopsy failure to recognize pulmonary embolism limited the accuracy of complication incidence estimates, while delayed symptoms of pulmonary infarction could also cause events that preceded treatment to be misclassified as complications occurring during early therapy.

The authors interpreted the 0.14% fatal pulmonary embolism rate during anticoagulant treatment of deep venous thrombosis as evidence that anticoagulant treatment substantially reduced pulmonary embolic mortality relative to historical untreated series.
The authors preferred more intensive anticoagulation with Quick prothrombin activity maintained below 30%, particularly for patients treated for pulmonary embolism.
The authors concluded that anticoagulants represented the treatment of choice for venous thromboembolism.
The authors concluded that recurrent thromboembolism in the first 12 weeks after hospital discharge could be reduced by continuing anticoagulant therapy for several months or more.
The authors recommended restricting operative treatment to patients in whom anticoagulants were contraindicated or in whom adequate anticoagulant therapy failed to prevent recurrent thromboembolism.
